posts.content_md:
Ok, I tore down my entire table and have begun to reconfigure it with a new geometry. The plan is to be able to shoot up to 8x10 master transmissions and up to 5x7 copies. I brought the old 16" collimator back onto the table and I cleaned it the best I could but it may not be good enough (poor baby is about 25 years old). It has very dim spots on it that I think are defects in the coating, corrosion? I may need to get it resurfaced. It's been a little challenging as the table is just under 4x8' and the collimator has a 75" focus. I did purchase a piece of front surface mirror that I can use between the spatial filter and the collimator. I used to have a contact on a collimator resurfacing company but I cannot seem to find it. Does anyone have a line on a resurfacing company?

Another reason for this post is I realized there is no real good information on table geometry for H1's and H2's on the Wiki. What I mean is information concerning how the H1 should be lit from the top or bottom in reference to the object. Once the plate is flipped it is illuminated from the opposite. This needs to be addressed with ones particular table geometry such that you do not end up with a final H2 that has a bottom reference beam.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
I guess the main thing to point out, which is not readily available in doing research, is that when you are making an H2 from and H1 the image from the H1 is the pseudoscopic image thus the H2 needs to be reference lit from the bottom such that you can turn the final hologram over and have it dispay the non pseudoscopic real image when illuminated from the conjucate top.

Whew... I think I said that right.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Ok, I thought I would post my geometry as that seems to be the thing most unavailable for other holographers. My table is about 3'7" by 7'6". So squeezing in everything is trying.

Here is the H1 to H2 set up alone (I simultaneously have the H1 with two object lightings on the table with just a drop out of one beam splitter I can go from one to the other). This is for a side reference beam, I deleted the overhead reference beam as I am now using my 12.5" (sorry, it was not 16" but 12.5") collimator instead of the flat overhead mirror used in my single beam set ups. Notice there is no beam splitter. Just a flat front surface intercepting mirror. With the thow prior to the interception and after, a collimator is not needed for the reference beam for the H2 as it is pretty far back. The black line at the top of the beam is blocker. The intercepting mirror is at the bottom and redirects part of the beam to the H2. The variable beam splitter is one of those cheap ones that gave double reflections (thin) but in this set up that is not a factor. It is placed in the path of the reflected reference beam for the H2. Thus by turning the variable beam splitter I can lower or raise the light level of the reference beam intensity thusly changing the ration of ref:obj in the copy set up. Pretty simple but very effective.

![Image](http://www.sketchys.com/HoloPage/HoloFiles/Illustrations/H2SetUp.jpg)

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md:
John-

Your geometry looks OK except for matching coherence length (CL). Looks like the path length for the H2 is much longer than for the H1. If your laser has very long CL, this is no problem, but matching CL in the copy setup is just as important as it is in the H1 setup.

Also, I typically shoot H1s with an overhead reference beam. Then for the copy setup I rotate the H1 90 degrees; rotate the laser polarization 90- degrees, and shoot it with side illumination and a side reference for the H2. I thought everybody did it this way...?

posts.author: Steve M
posts.content_md:
I see now that I miss read John's first two postings. I've found that my reference beam for H1 can be either overhead or from the side which I'm sure everyone already nows. I prefer a side reference beam because it gives me a lower center of gravity and greater stability. Either way though it doesn't have any thing to do with the reference beam for H2 other than possibly the setup path of the H1 reference beam getting in the way of the setup path for the H2 reference beam. You are absolutely right John that, assuming your real image is right side up relative to the table, a reference beam for H2 from underneath will give you overhead white light illumination.

At this point, one could bring up the problem of the wood grain effect when sandwiching film between glass plates, the orientation of p-polarization, and Brewster's angle, but my experience shows that when I use 8E75 or 649-F plates for sandwiching, the wood grain effect is essentially non-existant, probably because these plates are close to optically flat.

Hey Steve, I didn't respond because I wasn't sure what was being stated.

I must say I reconfigure my table in many different ways. The way below is to use the large collimator for an 8x10 to 5x7. It is a side set up because mounting the 14 inch by 2 inch thick collimator overhead has not been done yet. Also, I don't have a variable beam splitter other then the cheap attenuator which it good for throwing away light as in the below set up but to use it for beam splitting is bad as it causes dark interference fringes. 

I personally like the overhead set up better as my laser is polarized S, I can do single beams very easily as most objects are made to set upright, I can do single beams with the object lying down on it's back and I can do contact copies with one plate over the other laying flat with 3 blackened 1/4-20 screws separting them.

Then I use the overhead copy, which I posted some diagrams of which also does not need a "beam splitter". I made the Seahorses, dragon and elephant with that configuration. I find it very, very stable and easy to use.

I have plenty of power and no limits to coherence length so I guess I am able to not even address those would-be limitations.
